Tense negation Any bridi which involves tenses of selma'o PU, FAhA, or ZAhO can be contradicted by a _-nai_ suffixed to the tense cmavo. Some examples: **Example 10.129. ** mi | punai | klama | le | zarci ---|---|---|---|--- I | [past-not] | go-to | the | market. I didn't go to the market. --- As a contradictory negation, Example 10.129 implies that the bridi as a whole is false without saying anything about what is true. When the negated tense is a sumti tcita, _-nai_ negation indicates that the stated relationship does not hold: **Example 10.130. ** mi | klama | le | zarci | ca | nai ---|---|---|---|---|--- I | go-to | the | market | [present] | [not] le | nu | do | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|--- the | event-of | you | go-to | the | house. It is not true that I went to the market at the same time that you went to the house. --- **Example 10.131. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku | ne'inai | le | kumfa ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog | [within-not] | the | room. The man didn't bite the dog inside the room. --- **Example 10.132. ** mi | morsi | ca'onai | le | nu | mi | jmive ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | am-dead | [continuitive-negated] | the | event-of | I | live. It is false that I am dead during my life. --- It is also possible to perform scalar negation of whole tense constructs by placing a member of NAhE before them. Unlike contradictory negation, scalar negation asserts a truth: that the bridi is true with some tense other than that specified. The following examples are scalar negation analogues of Example 10.129 to Example 10.131: **Example 10.133. ** mi | na'e | pu | klama | le | zarci ---|---|---|---|---|--- I | [non-] | [past] | go-to | the | market. I go to the market other than in the past. --- **Example 10.134. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku | to'e | ne'i | le | kumfa ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog | [opposite-of] | [within] | the | room. The man bites the dog outside the room. --- **Example 10.135. ** mi | klama | le | zarci | na'e | ca | le | nu ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | go-to | the | market | [non-] | [present] | the | event-of do | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|--- you | go-to | the | house. I went to the market at a time other than the time at which you went to the house. --- **Example 10.136. ** mi | morsi | na'e | ca'o | le | nu | mi | jmive ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | am-dead | [non-] | [continuitive] | the | event-of | I | live. I am dead other than during my life. --- Unlike _-nai_ contradictory negation, scalar negation of tenses is not limited to PU and FAhA: **Example 10.137. ** le | verba | na'e | ri'u | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | child | [non-] | [right] | walks-on | the | ice The child walks on the ice other than to my right. --- The use of _-nai_ on cmavo of TAhE and ROI has already been discussed in Section 10.9; this use is also a scalar negation. * * * Chapter 10. Tense relations between sentences The sumti tcita method, explained in Section 10.12, of asserting a tense relationship between two events suffers from asymmetry. Specifically, **Example 10.109. ** le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | child | | walks-on | the | ice zu'a | le | nu | le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [left] | the | event-of | the | man | | bites | the | dog. The child walks on the ice to the left of where the man bites the dog. --- which specifies an imaginary journey leftward from the man biting the dog to the child walking on the ice, claims only that the child walks on the ice. By the nature of _le nu_ , the man's biting the dog is merely referred to without being claimed. If it seems desirable to claim both, each event can be expressed as a main sentence bridi, with a special form of __i__ connecting them: **Example 10.110. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .izu'abo | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left, the child walks on the ice. --- _.izu'abo_ is a compound cmavo: the __i__ separates the sentences and the __zu'a__ is the tense. The __bo__ is required to prevent the __zu'a__ from gobbling up the following sumti, namely _le verba_. Note that the bridi in Example 10.110 appear in the reverse order from their appearance in Example 10.109. With _.izu'abo_ (and all other afterthought tense connectives) the sentence specifying the origin of the journey comes first. This is a natural order for sentences, but requires some care when converting between this form and the sumti tcita form. Example 10.110 means the same thing as: **Example 10.111. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku | .i | zu'a | la'edi'u ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. | | [Left] | the-referent-of-the-last-sentence le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|--- the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. Left of what I just mentioned, the child walks on the ice. --- If the __bo__ is omitted in Example 10.110, the meaning changes: **Example 10.112. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'a | le | verba | cu | | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | [something] | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left of the child, something walks on the ice. --- Here the first place of the second sentence is unspecified, because __zu'a__ has absorbed the sumti _le verba_. Do not confuse either Example 10.110 or Example 10.112 with the following: **Example 10.113. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'aku | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. Left of me, the child walks on the ice. --- In Example 10.113, the origin point is the speaker, as is usual with _zu'aku_. Example 10.110 makes the origin point of the tense the event described by the first sentence. Two sentences may also be connected in forethought by a tense relationship. Just like afterthought tense connection, forethought tense connection claims both sentences, and in addition claims that the time or space relationship specified by the tense holds between the events the two sentences describe. The origin sentence is placed first, preceded by a tense plus __gi__. Another __gi__ is used to separate the sentences: **Example 10.114. ** pugi | mi | klama | le | zarci | gi | mi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [past] | I | go-to | the | market | [,] | I | go-to | the | house. Before I go to the market, I go to the house. --- A parallel construction can be used to express a tense relationship between sumti: **Example 10.115. ** mi | klama | pugi | le | zarci | gi | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | go-to | [past] | the | market | [,] | the | house. Because English does not have any direct way of expressing a tense-like relationship between nouns, Example 10.115 cannot be expressed in English without paraphrasing it either into Example 10.114 or else into “I go to the house before the market”, which is ambiguous – is the market going? Finally, a third forethought construction expresses a tense relationship between bridi-tails rather than whole bridi. (The construct known as a “bridi-tail” is explained fully in Section 14.9; roughly speaking, it is a selbri, possibly with following sumti.) Example 10.116 is equivalent in meaning to Example 10.114 and Example 10.115: **Example 10.116. ** mi | pugi | klama | le | zarci | gi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | [past] | go-to | the | market | [,] | go-to | the | house. I, before going to the market, go to the house. --- In both Example 10.115 and Example 10.116, the underlying sentences _mi klama le zarci_ and _mi klama le zdani_ are not claimed; only the relationship in time between them is claimed. Both the forethought and the afterthought forms are appropriate with PU, ZI, FAhA, VA, and ZAhO tenses. In all cases, the equivalent forms are (where X and Y stand for sentences, and TENSE for a tense cmavo): subordinate | X TENSE le nu Y ---|--- afterthought coordinate | Y .i+TENSE+bo X forethought coordinate | TENSE+gi X gi Y * * * Chapter 10. Indicators Different cultures express emotions and attitudes with a variety of intonations and gestures that are not usually included in written language. Some of these are available in some languages as interjections (i.e. “Aha!”, “Oh no!”, “Ouch!”, “Aahh!”, etc.), but they vary greatly from culture to culture. Lojban has a group of cmavo known as “attitudinal indicators” which specifically covers this type of commentary on spoken statements. They are both written and spoken, but require no specific intonation or gestures. Grammatically they are very simple: one or more attitudinals at the beginning of a bridi apply to the entire bridi; anywhere else in the bridi they apply to the word immediately to the left. For example: **Example 2.79. ** .ie | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Agreement! | I | - | go. Yep! I'll go. --- **Example 2.80. ** .ei | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Obligation! | I | - | go. I should go. --- **Example 2.81. ** mi | [cu] | klama | le melbi ---|---|---|--- I | - | go | to-the beautiful-thing .ui | [ku] ---|--- and I am happy because it is the beautiful thing I'm going to | - Not all indicators indicate attitudes. Discursives, another group of cmavo with the same grammatical rules as attitudinal indicators, allow free expression of certain kinds of commentary about the main utterances. Using discursives allows a clear separation of these so-called “metalinguistic” features from the underlying statements and logical structure. By comparison, the English words “but” and “also”, which discursively indicate contrast or an added weight of example, are logically equivalent to “and”, which does not have a discursive content. The average English-speaker does not think about, and may not even realize, the paradoxical idea that “but” basically means “and”. **Example 2.82. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | You | - | stay. **Example 2.83. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ji'a | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | In addition, | you | - | stay. | added weight **Example 2.84. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ku'i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | However, | you | - | stay. | contrast Another group of indicators are called “evidentials”. Evidentials show the speaker's relationship to the statement, specifically how the speaker came to make the statement. These include __za'a__ (I directly observe the relationship), __pe'i__ (I believe that the relationship holds), __ru'a__ (I postulate the relationship), and others. Many American Indian languages use this kind of words. **Example 2.85. ** pe'i | do | [cu] | melbi ---|---|---|--- I opine! | You | - | are beautiful. **Example 2.86. ** za'a | do | [cu] | melbi ---|---|---|--- I directly observe! | You | - | are beautiful. * * * Chapter 2. A Quick Tour of Lojban Grammar, With Diagrams --- Prev: Section 2.10 | Next: Section 2.12 ---|--- Table of Contents Book Info Page * * * ## 2.11. Examples of brivla The simplest form of selbri is an individual word. A word which may by itself express a selbri relation is called a __brivla__. The three types of brivla are gismu (root words), lujvo (compounds), and fu'ivla (borrowings from other languages). All have identical grammatical uses. So far, most of our selbri have been gismu or tanru built from gismu. gismu: **Example 2.46. ** mi | [cu] | klama | ti | zo'e | zo'e | ta ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- Go-er | - | goes | destination | origin | route | means. I go here (to this) using that means (from somewhere via some route). --- lujvo: **Example 2.47. ** ta | [cu] | blari'o ---|---|--- That | - | is-blue-green. fu'ivla: **Example 2.48. ** ti | [cu] | djarspageti ---|---|--- This | - | is-spaghetti. Some cmavo may also serve as selbri, acting as variables that stand for another selbri. The most commonly used of these is __go'i__ , which represents the main bridi of the previous Lojban sentence, with any new sumti or other sentence features being expressed replacing the previously expressed ones. Thus, in this context: **Example 2.49. ** ta | [cu] | go'i ---|---|--- That | - | too/same-as-last selbri. That (is spaghetti), too. --- * * * Chapter 2. 1. Debater_B’s summary of Lojban word order (“le [noun] cu [verb] [noun]”) in Sentence 4 is an oversimplification and thus flawed. Lojban permits a variety of selbri–sumti orders, as long as the roles are unambiguously marked. The only strict requirement is that if a selbri is not first, it must be preceded by a terminator or by the separator <u>cu</u> when the first sumti would otherwise be mistaken for the selbri.  
   • In fact, any sumti can appear after the selbri so long as the grammatical relations remain clear: you can have “[sumti₁] [sumti₂] cu [selbri] ([sumti₃] …)” (see Section 2.16: indicators and sumti order).  
   • Thus the statement “(B) does not follow the structure ‘le [noun] cu [verb] [noun]’” is false: “nicte loldi cu le jdika” is equally of the form “sumti₁ sumti₂ cu selbri sumti₃,” with “nicte loldi” filling two sumti places and “le jdika” the third.

2. Debater_B’s categorization of “nicte jdika” in (A) as a coherent compound meaning “nightly decrease” ignores that Lojban compounds must obey tanru precedence rules, and there is no rule that cumulated adjectives must immediately follow the selbri.  
   • In the gismu definitions, “nicte” is a selbri meaning “x₁ is nighttime of day x₂ at location x₃,” while “jdika” means “x₁ decreases/contracts x₂ by amount x₃.” Placing them back-to-back makes a tanru, but it is not guaranteed to mean “nightly decrease.” Without an explicit framing sumti structure, “nicte jdika” is ambiguous: is the night doing the decreasing, or the floor experiencing a nightly decrease? Debater_B fails to acknowledge this ambiguity.

3. Debater_B’s claim in Sentence 4 that (B) “does not follow [the] structure correctly” is thus unfounded. Both (A) and (B) fit the same selbri–sumti template. The real question is which selbri and sumti roles convey the intended meaning, not a simplistic pattern check.  
   • If one wanted to express “the nighttime decreases the floor,” choice (B) “nicte loldi cu le jdika” would actually be more literal: sumti “nicte” (night) acts on “loldi” (floor) as object, yielding “The night causes the floor to diminish by amount the decrease,” which is a coherent claim.  
   • By contrast, (A)’s “le loldi cu nicte jdika” more naturally reads “The floor experiences nighttime shrinking,” but even that requires that “nicte” take two sumti (the event-of-night and location), which Debater_B never analyzes.

4. Finally, Sentence 4 commits the serious flaw of appealing to an unsubstantiated “typical” structure as though it were a rule. Lojban grammar, per the official reference, has no canonical “noun–cu–verb–noun” monopoly. By invoking a nonexistent rule, Debater_B’s Sentence 4 is logically unsound.  

Conclusion: Sentence 4 is flawed because it misstates Lojban’s word-order rules, ignores the semantic ambiguity of the tanru “nicte jdika,” and appeals to a false “typical” structure.

Indicators Different cultures express emotions and attitudes with a variety of intonations and gestures that are not usually included in written language. Using discursives allows a clear separation of these so-called “metalinguistic” features from the underlying statements and logical structure. By comparison, the English words “but” and “also”, which discursively indicate contrast or an added weight of example, are logically equivalent to “and”, which does not have a discursive content. 1. Sentence 4 Misstates What Counts as “Following the Template”  
   Debater B insists that only structure “sumti₁ CU selbri [sumti₂ …]” is grammatical, and therefore (B) “does not follow the structure” because its selbri appears to be “LE jdika.” But this claim collapses two distinct issues—form versus function—and so is itself flawed.  
   • Formally, both (A) and (B) fit the pattern sumti₁ CU selbri sumti₂:  
     – (A) sumti₁=le loldi, CU, selbri=nicte jdika, (implicit) sumti₂…  
     – (B) sumti₁=nicte loldi, CU, selbri=le jdika  
   • Debater B’s assertion that “LE jdika” cannot serve as a selbri is beside the point. It is true that LE always flags a sumti (<invalid_quote>LE marks a sumti, not a predicate</invalid_quote>), but that simply shows (B) has an unambiguously marked sumti in the selbri slot—exactly the same misplacement of LE that Sentence 4 claims to detect! In other words, Debater B has trapped themselves: if LE jdika is indeed a sumti, then (B) still “follows the template” structurally, but merely mis‐assigns roles. Sentence 4 fails to account for this nuance.

2. Sentence 4 Ignores Tanru Valence Mismatch  
   Sentence 4 treats “nicte jdika” as a neat two‐word selbri (“night‐decrease”), whereas in fact each gismu has its own three‐place structure:  
     – nicte: x₁ is nighttime of day x₂ at location x₃  
     – jdika: x₁ decreases/contracts property x₂ by amount x₃  
   Simply juxtaposing them does not magically resolve their valences into a single two‐place predicate. A proper Lojban compound (lujvo) would require morphological combining or explicit sumti‐connection to satisfy all six places. By ignoring this, Sentence 4 presents a false simplicity.

3. Sentence 4 Relies on an Unstated “Typical” That Doesn’t Exist  
   Debater B’s Sentence 4 appeals to a “typical” bridi shape as though it were a hard rule. But the reference grammar never endorses “noun–CU–verb–noun” as a canonical form. All it says is:  
   <invalid_quote>CU is an elidable marker: separates selbri from preceding sumti…</invalid_quote>  
   It never prohibits additional sumti before or after, nor mandates exactly one sumti on each side. By invoking a nonexistent rule, Sentence 4 is logically unsound.

4. Sentence 4 Confuses Surface Order with Underlying Grammatical Roles  
   Finally, by branding (B) “incorrect” solely because it looks different on the surface, Sentence 4 conflates linear order with deep structure. In fact, Lojban allows both forethought and afterthought connections, tanru stacking, and variable sumti–selbri placements (Sections 10.16, 10.17). A correct analysis must consider CMAVO like BO, GI, and NU to pin down what is being claimed. Sentence 4 does none of this—it simply reads word order off English prejudices.

Conclusion  
Sentence 4 is flawed because it:  
 1. Mistakes the presence of LE in (B) for a rule‐violation rather than a misassignment of grammatical role.  
 2. Fails to address how two three‐place gismu compose into a single predicate.  
 3. Invents a “typical” structure absent from the reference grammar.  
 4. Conflates surface word order with valid Lojban mechanisms for indicating relations.  

Therefore, the claim “(B) does not follow the structure” rests on misconceptions and unsubstantiated premises. Sentence 4 is not a correct analysis of Lojban grammar.

Tense relations between sentences The sumti tcita method, explained in Section 10.12, of asserting a tense relationship between two events suffers from asymmetry. Specifically, **Example 10.109. ** le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | child | | walks-on | the | ice zu'a | le | nu | le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [left] | the | event-of | the | man | | bites | the | dog. The child walks on the ice to the left of where the man bites the dog. --- which specifies an imaginary journey leftward from the man biting the dog to the child walking on the ice, claims only that the child walks on the ice. By the nature of _le nu_ , the man's biting the dog is merely referred to without being claimed. If it seems desirable to claim both, each event can be expressed as a main sentence bridi, with a special form of __i__ connecting them: **Example 10.110. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .izu'abo | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left, the child walks on the ice. --- _.izu'abo_ is a compound cmavo: the __i__ separates the sentences and the __zu'a__ is the tense. The __bo__ is required to prevent the __zu'a__ from gobbling up the following sumti, namely _le verba_. Note that the bridi in Example 10.110 appear in the reverse order from their appearance in Example 10.109. With _.izu'abo_ (and all other afterthought tense connectives) the sentence specifying the origin of the journey comes first. This is a natural order for sentences, but requires some care when converting between this form and the sumti tcita form. Example 10.110 means the same thing as: **Example 10.111. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku | .i | zu'a | la'edi'u ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. | | [Left] | the-referent-of-the-last-sentence le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|--- the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. Left of what I just mentioned, the child walks on the ice. --- If the __bo__ is omitted in Example 10.110, the meaning changes: **Example 10.112. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'a | le | verba | cu | | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | [something] | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left of the child, something walks on the ice. --- Here the first place of the second sentence is unspecified, because __zu'a__ has absorbed the sumti _le verba_. Do not confuse either Example 10.110 or Example 10.112 with the following: **Example 10.113. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'aku | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. Left of me, the child walks on the ice. --- In Example 10.113, the origin point is the speaker, as is usual with _zu'aku_. Example 10.110 makes the origin point of the tense the event described by the first sentence. Two sentences may also be connected in forethought by a tense relationship. Just like afterthought tense connection, forethought tense connection claims both sentences, and in addition claims that the time or space relationship specified by the tense holds between the events the two sentences describe. The origin sentence is placed first, preceded by a tense plus __gi__. Another __gi__ is used to separate the sentences: **Example 10.114. ** pugi | mi | klama | le | zarci | gi | mi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [past] | I | go-to | the | market | [,] | I | go-to | the | house. Before I go to the market, I go to the house. --- A parallel construction can be used to express a tense relationship between sumti: **Example 10.115. ** mi | klama | pugi | le | zarci | gi | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | go-to | [past] | the | market | [,] | the | house. Because English does not have any direct way of expressing a tense-like relationship between nouns, Example 10.115 cannot be expressed in English without paraphrasing it either into Example 10.114 or else into “I go to the house before the market”, which is ambiguous – is the market going? Finally, a third forethought construction expresses a tense relationship between bridi-tails rather than whole bridi. (The construct known as a “bridi-tail” is explained fully in Section 14.9; roughly speaking, it is a selbri, possibly with following sumti.) Example 10.116 is equivalent in meaning to Example 10.114 and Example 10.115: **Example 10.116. ** mi | pugi | klama | le | zarci | gi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | [past] | go-to | the | market | [,] | go-to | the | house. I, before going to the market, go to the house. --- In both Example 10.115 and Example 10.116, the underlying sentences _mi klama le zarci_ and _mi klama le zdani_ are not claimed; only the relationship in time between them is claimed. Both the forethought and the afterthought forms are appropriate with PU, ZI, FAhA, VA, and ZAhO tenses. Indicators Different cultures express emotions and attitudes with a variety of intonations and gestures that are not usually included in written language. Some of these are available in some languages as interjections (i.e. “Aha!”, “Oh no!”, “Ouch!”, “Aahh!”, etc.), but they vary greatly from culture to culture. Lojban has a group of cmavo known as “attitudinal indicators” which specifically covers this type of commentary on spoken statements. They are both written and spoken, but require no specific intonation or gestures. Grammatically they are very simple: one or more attitudinals at the beginning of a bridi apply to the entire bridi; anywhere else in the bridi they apply to the word immediately to the left. For example: **Example 2.79. ** .ie | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Agreement! | I | - | go. Yep! I'll go. --- **Example 2.80. ** .ei | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Obligation! | I | - | go. I should go. --- **Example 2.81. ** mi | [cu] | klama | le melbi ---|---|---|--- I | - | go | to-the beautiful-thing .ui | [ku] ---|--- and I am happy because it is the beautiful thing I'm going to | - Not all indicators indicate attitudes. Discursives, another group of cmavo with the same grammatical rules as attitudinal indicators, allow free expression of certain kinds of commentary about the main utterances. Using discursives allows a clear separation of these so-called “metalinguistic” features from the underlying statements and logical structure. By comparison, the English words “but” and “also”, which discursively indicate contrast or an added weight of example, are logically equivalent to “and”, which does not have a discursive content. The average English-speaker does not think about, and may not even realize, the paradoxical idea that “but” basically means “and”. **Example 2.82. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | You | - | stay. **Example 2.83. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ji'a | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | In addition, | you | - | stay. | added weight **Example 2.84. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ku'i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | However, | you | - | stay. | contrast Another group of indicators are called “evidentials”. Evidentials show the speaker's relationship to the statement, specifically how the speaker came to make the statement. These include __za'a__ (I directly observe the relationship), __pe'i__ (I believe that the relationship holds), __ru'a__ (I postulate the relationship), and others. Debater_A’s critique of Sentence 4 rests on three misunderstandings: (1) what Sentence 4 actually claims, (2) how CU works, and (3) the roles of sumti vs. selbri. My refutation:

1. Sentence 4 does _not_ claim that “le [noun] cu [verb] [noun]” is the _only_ legal word‐order in Lojban, only that it is the _typical_ template for a one‐place bridi with two arguments.  In Lojban’s simplest bridi of the form  
   sumti₁   CU   selbri   sumti₂  
   the first argument (sumti₁) comes before CU, CU marks the start of the predicate, the selbri comes next, then its remaining place‐fillers follow.  That is exactly what Sentence 4 says.  Debater_A attacks a straw man by insisting Lojban allows every conceivable variation _after_ CU—but Sentence 4 is describing the _archetype_ of a “[noun]–CU–verb–noun” bridi, not forbidding other more complex orders.

2. CU’s sole function is to separate the _preceding_ sumti(s) from the selbri.  As the background defines it:  
   <quote>n': 'elidable marker: separates selbri from preceding sumti,</quote>  
   You cannot start a selbri without CU if a sumti appears first, or the parser will treat your first word as the selbri.  Sentence 4 correctly identifies this: in (A), “le loldi” is sumti₁, CU marks the boundary, then “nicte jdika” is the selbri (a tanru of two gismu).  In (B), though there _is_ CU, the part before it—“nicte loldi”—is not a single sumti₁ but two gismu in sequence, with neither marked as a selbri by any CU‐equivalent.  Debater_A’s claim that “nicte loldi cu le jdika” is just “sumti₁ sumti₂ cu selbri sumti₃” ignores that _every_ selbri must be preceded by CU (or a terminator) if there is any sumti before it.  In (B), the parser reads “nicte” as selbri (because it sees a gismu in selbri‐slot), so “loldi” becomes an unmarked sumti in the selbri‐slot—_ungrammatical_.  Sentence 4’s simple pattern check is exactly how one spots that error.

3. Tanru ambiguity does _not_ invalidate the pattern claim of Sentence 4.  Whether “nicte jdika” means “nightly decrease” or “decrease of night” is a semantic question about brivla combination, but it does not change the fact that in (A) those two brivla form the selbri.  Debater_A complains of “ambiguity” here, but that has no bearing on whether Sentence 4 correctly identifies that (A) follows the sumti–CU–selbri template and (B) does not.  The question we’re judging is whether Sentence 4 is _grammatically_ correct, not whether it resolves every semantic nuance of “nicte jdika.”

Because Sentence 4 accurately states the _standard_ form of a one‐verb, two‐argument bridi and correctly applies it to show that (A) slots into sumti–CU–selbri while (B) mangles the boundary between sumti and selbri, Sentence 4 is _correct_. 1. Sentence 4 does _not_ claim that “le [noun] cu [verb] [noun]” is the _only_ legal word‐order in Lojban, only that it is the _typical_ template for a one‐place bridi with two arguments.  In Lojban’s simplest bridi of the form  
   sumti₁   CU   selbri   sumti₂  
   the first argument (sumti₁) comes before CU, CU marks the start of the predicate, the selbri comes next, then its remaining place‐fillers follow.  That is exactly what Sentence 4 says.  Debater_A attacks a straw man by insisting Lojban allows every conceivable variation _after_ CU—but Sentence 4 is describing the _archetype_ of a “[noun]–CU–verb–noun” bridi, not forbidding other more complex orders.

2. CU’s sole function is to separate the _preceding_ sumti(s) from the selbri.  As the background defines it:  
   <quote>CU: “elidable marker: separates selbri from preceding sumti”</quote>  
   You cannot start a selbri without CU if a sumti appears first, or the parser will treat your first word as the selbri.  Sentence 4 correctly identifies this: in (A), “le loldi” is sumti₁, CU marks the boundary, then “nicte jdika” is the selbri (a tanru of two gismu).  In (B), though there _is_ CU, the part before it—“nicte loldi”—is not a single sumti₁ but two gismu in sequence, with neither marked as a selbri by any CU‐equivalent.  Debater_A’s claim that “nicte loldi cu le jdika” is just “sumti₁ sumti₂ cu selbri sumti₃” ignores that _every_ selbri must be preceded by CU (or a terminator) if there is any sumti before it.  In (B), the parser reads “nicte” as selbri (because it sees a gismu in selbri‐slot), so “loldi” becomes an unmarked sumti in the selbri‐slot—_ungrammatical_.  Sentence 4’s simple pattern check is exactly how one spots that error.

3. Tanru ambiguity does _not_ invalidate the pattern claim of Sentence 4.  Whether “nicte jdika” means “nightly decrease” or “decrease of night” is a semantic question about brivla combination, but it does not change the fact that in (A) those two brivla form the selbri.  Debater_A complains of “ambiguity” here, but that has no bearing on whether Sentence 4 correctly identifies that (A) follows the sumti–CU–selbri template and (B) does not.  The question we’re judging is whether Sentence 4 is _grammatically_ correct, not whether it resolves every semantic nuance of “nicte jdika.”

Because Sentence 4 accurately states the _standard_ form of a one‐verb, two‐argument bridi and correctly applies it to show that (A) slots into sumti–CU–selbri while (B) mangles the boundary between sumti and selbri, Sentence 4 is _correct_. Debater_A’s objections either dispute a claim Sentence 4 never made or confuse semantic ambiguity with syntactic form.

Tense negation Any bridi which involves tenses of selma'o PU, FAhA, or ZAhO can be contradicted by a _-nai_ suffixed to the tense cmavo. When the negated tense is a sumti tcita, _-nai_ negation indicates that the stated relationship does not hold: **Example 10.130. ** mi | klama | le | zarci | ca | nai ---|---|---|---|---|--- I | go-to | the | market | [present] | [not] le | nu | do | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|--- the | event-of | you | go-to | the | house. Unlike contradictory negation, scalar negation asserts a truth: that the bridi is true with some tense other than that specified. Tense relations between sentences The sumti tcita method, explained in Section 10.12, of asserting a tense relationship between two events suffers from asymmetry. By the nature of _le nu_ , the man's biting the dog is merely referred to without being claimed. If it seems desirable to claim both, each event can be expressed as a main sentence bridi, with a special form of __i__ connecting them: **Example 10.110. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .izu'abo | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left, the child walks on the ice. --- _.izu'abo_ is a compound cmavo: the __i__ separates the sentences and the __zu'a__ is the tense. The __bo__ is required to prevent the __zu'a__ from gobbling up the following sumti, namely _le verba_. Note that the bridi in Example 10.110 appear in the reverse order from their appearance in Example 10.109. With _.izu'abo_ (and all other afterthought tense connectives) the sentence specifying the origin of the journey comes first. This is a natural order for sentences, but requires some care when converting between this form and the sumti tcita form. Example 10.110 means the same thing as: **Example 10.111. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku | .i | zu'a | la'edi'u ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. | | [Left] | the-referent-of-the-last-sentence le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|--- the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. Left of what I just mentioned, the child walks on the ice. --- If the __bo__ is omitted in Example 10.110, the meaning changes: **Example 10.112. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'a | le | verba | cu | | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | [something] | walks-on | the | ice. The man bites the dog. To the left of the child, something walks on the ice. --- Here the first place of the second sentence is unspecified, because __zu'a__ has absorbed the sumti _le verba_. Do not confuse either Example 10.110 or Example 10.112 with the following: **Example 10.113. ** le | nanmu | cu | batci | le | gerku ---|---|---|---|---|--- The | man | | bites | the | dog. .i | zu'aku | le | verba | cu | cadzu | le | bisli ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- | [Left] | the | child | | walks-on | the | ice. Just like afterthought tense connection, forethought tense connection claims both sentences, and in addition claims that the time or space relationship specified by the tense holds between the events the two sentences describe. The origin sentence is placed first, preceded by a tense plus __gi__. Another __gi__ is used to separate the sentences: **Example 10.114. ** pugi | mi | klama | le | zarci | gi | mi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- [past] | I | go-to | the | market | [,] | I | go-to | the | house. (The construct known as a “bridi-tail” is explained fully in Section 14.9; roughly speaking, it is a selbri, possibly with following sumti.) Example 10.116 is equivalent in meaning to Example 10.114 and Example 10.115: **Example 10.116. ** mi | pugi | klama | le | zarci | gi | klama | le | zdani ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | [past] | go-to | the | market | [,] | go-to | the | house. Indicators Different cultures express emotions and attitudes with a variety of intonations and gestures that are not usually included in written language. Some of these are available in some languages as interjections (i.e. “Aha!”, “Oh no!”, “Ouch!”, “Aahh!”, etc.), but they vary greatly from culture to culture. Lojban has a group of cmavo known as “attitudinal indicators” which specifically covers this type of commentary on spoken statements. They are both written and spoken, but require no specific intonation or gestures. Grammatically they are very simple: one or more attitudinals at the beginning of a bridi apply to the entire bridi; anywhere else in the bridi they apply to the word immediately to the left. For example: **Example 2.79. ** .ie | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Agreement! | I | - | go. Yep! I'll go. --- **Example 2.80. ** .ei | mi | [cu] | klama ---|---|---|--- Obligation! | I | - | go. I should go. --- **Example 2.81. ** mi | [cu] | klama | le melbi ---|---|---|--- I | - | go | to-the beautiful-thing .ui | [ku] ---|--- and I am happy because it is the beautiful thing I'm going to | - Not all indicators indicate attitudes. Discursives, another group of cmavo with the same grammatical rules as attitudinal indicators, allow free expression of certain kinds of commentary about the main utterances. Using discursives allows a clear separation of these so-called “metalinguistic” features from the underlying statements and logical structure. By comparison, the English words “but” and “also”, which discursively indicate contrast or an added weight of example, are logically equivalent to “and”, which does not have a discursive content. The average English-speaker does not think about, and may not even realize, the paradoxical idea that “but” basically means “and”. **Example 2.82. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | You | - | stay. **Example 2.83. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ji'a | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | In addition, | you | - | stay. | added weight **Example 2.84. ** mi | [cu] | klama | .i | ku'i | do | [cu] | stali ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|--- I | - | go. | | However, | you | - | stay. | contrast Another group of indicators are called “evidentials”. Evidentials show the speaker's relationship to the statement, specifically how the speaker came to make the statement. These include __za'a__ (I directly observe the relationship), __pe'i__ (I believe that the relationship holds), __ru'a__ (I postulate the relationship), and others.
